brief.topic: The Shortcut That Makes Everyone Slower

s01: A new shortcut opens.
Every driver chooses a faster route for themselves.
Somehow, everyone ends up slower.
Here is an ideal traffic network with four thousand drivers.
The two teal road sections take one minute for every hundred drivers using them.
Each coral section always takes forty five minutes.
Without a shortcut, traffic splits evenly between the two routes.
Each driver spends twenty minutes on a teal section, then forty five on a coral one.
Sixty five minutes altogether.
Now connect the two middle junctions with a zero minute shortcut.
That is an idealization, not a realistic road length.
A teal section never takes more than forty minutes, even with all four thousand drivers.
So each driver prefers using both teal sections and skipping the forty five minute sections.
Everyone makes that choice.
Both teal sections now carry all four thousand drivers.
Forty plus forty is eighty minutes.
The shortcut has made the stable outcome fifteen minutes slower.
One driver cannot fix this by switching back.
Their alternative takes forty plus forty five: eighty five minutes.
The old sixty five minute arrangement is still possible if everyone coordinates to ignore the shortcut.
More options did not remove it.
They changed the incentives.
This is Braess's paradox: a better choice for each person need not create a better outcome together.

scenes.narration:
A new shortcut opens. Every driver chooses a faster route for themselves. Somehow, everyone ends up slower.

Here is an ideal traffic network with four thousand drivers. The two teal road sections take one minute for every hundred drivers using them. Each coral section always takes forty five minutes.

Without a shortcut, traffic splits evenly between the two routes. Each driver spends twenty minutes on a teal section, then forty five on a coral one. Sixty five minutes altogether.

Now connect the two middle junctions with a zero minute shortcut. That is an idealization, not a realistic road length.

A teal section never takes more than forty minutes, even with all four thousand drivers. So each driver prefers using both teal sections and skipping the forty five minute sections.

Everyone makes that choice. Both teal sections now carry all four thousand drivers. Forty plus forty is eighty minutes. The shortcut has made the stable outcome fifteen minutes slower.

One driver cannot fix this by switching back. Their alternative takes forty plus forty five: eighty five minutes.

The old sixty five minute arrangement is still possible if everyone coordinates to ignore the shortcut. More options did not remove it. They changed the incentives. This is Braess's paradox: a better choice for each person need not create a better outcome together.
